title: The Power of Proper Quoting 🛡️
description: Master quoting rules – double vs single, escaping, and how they prevent injection and word splitting.

slides.title: Quoting: Your First Line of Defence 🔐
slides.content:
## Why Quotes Matter

Quotes control how Bash interprets spaces and special characters. Without them, your script can behave unpredictably – opening doors to injection attacks.

- Double quotes `" "` allow variable expansion but prevent word splitting and globbing.
- Single quotes `' '` suppress all expansion.
- Backslash `\` escapes a single character.

**Golden Rule**: always double‑quote variable expansions unless you explicitly want word splitting.

slides.title: The Unquoted Disaster 💥
slides.content: Imagine a file named `my file.txt` – unquoted `$f` splits into two words!
slides.codeSnippet:
f="my file.txt"
# BAD: ls $f tries to list 'my' and 'file.txt'
ls $f
# GOOD: ls "$f" treats it as one argument
ls "$f"

quizData.question: What happens when you use `rm $file` and `$file` contains spaces?

options.text: It may attempt to delete multiple files (word splitting)
It fails with a syntax error

quizData.explanation: Unquoted expansions undergo word splitting, so a filename with spaces becomes multiple arguments, potentially deleting unintended files.

slides.title: Double Quotes Save Variables 🧾
slides.content:
## Preserve the Original Value

Double quotes keep the expanded value as a single argument. They also prevent globbing (`*` and `?` are not expanded).

```bash
echo "$var"           # safe
grep "$pattern" file  # safe
```
Even if you think the variable won't contain spaces, defensive quoting costs nothing.

slides.title: Glob Expansion Blocked
slides.content: Without quotes, a variable containing `*` can wreak havoc:
slides.codeSnippet:
pattern="*"
# BAD: echo $pattern lists all files!
# GOOD:
echo "$pattern"

quizData.question: Double quotes prevent variable expansion.
quizData.explanation: Double quotes still allow variable (`$var`) and command (`$(cmd)`) expansion; they only suppress word splitting and globbing.

slides.title: Single Quotes: Literal Fortress 🏰
slides.content:
## When You Need Raw Strings

Single quotes lock everything inside – no variable, command, or escape is processed (except a single quote can't appear inside single quotes).

Use them for:
- Fixed strings with special characters
- Awk/sed scripts where `$` has different meaning
- Passing regex patterns to grep that contain `$`

slides.title: Single vs Double Demo
slides.codeSnippet:
price=5
echo "The cost is $price"  # The cost is 5
echo 'The cost is $price'  # The cost is $price

slides.title: Escaping with Backslash ✂️
slides.content:
## Disable a Single Character

To include a literal quote or dollar sign inside double quotes, escape it: `"He said \"hello\""`.

A backslash at the end of a line continues the command on the next line (line continuation).

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content: Use `printf '%q' "$var"` to see how Bash would quote a string safely for reuse – perfect for logging variables with special characters.
